entries.title: William J. Quinlan, son of Richard J. Daley's corporation counsel, joins crowded race for mayor
entries.summary: <p>Billing himself as a reformer who “understands the system, but is not part of the system,” attorney William J. Quinlan is joining the crowded race for mayor of Chicago.</p><p>Quinlan’s father and namesake was the ultimate Chicago insider having served as city corporation counsel under former Mayor Richard J. Daley.</p><p>Quinlan followed in his father’s footsteps, spending three years as general counsel for Illinois until the arrest of now-convicted, then-Gov. Rod Blagojevich. He went on to serve as an election attorney for leading Democrats, including in the 2012 re-election campaign of then-President Barack Obama, and as an attorney for fired former Chicago Public Schools CEO Pedro Martinez.</p><p>As a child, the younger Quinlan also survived a devastating family tragedy.</p><p>His mother and younger brother were killed in a fire at the Quinlan family’s Sauganash home. Quinlan life was saved by Northwest Side neighbors whom he credits with having risked their own lives to save his.</p><p>Another brother died after struggling with mental illness and “navigating a fragmented system of care.” Quinlan also lost a grandfather to gun violence. He says he emerged from those family tragedies as a stronger, more empathetic leader.</p><p>"A lot of people have had a lot of tragedies. I've had a fair amount in my life. And what that taught me is we're all here for the grace of God," Quinlan, 56, told the Sun-Times. "I lost many, many family members in tragic circumstances. And I realized that life is to be cherished. It comes with it an obligation to give back. Even though I have a thriving legal practice, we all have an obligation to try and make Chicago better." </p><p>Quinlan said he had a front-row seat to the dysfunction at Brandon Johnson's City Hall while donating his time to represent Martinez after the mayor fired the CPS CEO.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/13/chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson-announcement-reelection-bid-2027" >Mayor Johnson embarks on reelection bid, says he’s best choice in race between ‘real progressives and posers’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>"What we had was a mayor not acting on behalf of the children, not acting on behalf of the citizens, but acting on behalf of himself and his political gain by helping the special interest that got him elected," Quinlan said, referring to the Chicago Teachers Union that helped put Johnson in office. "I stood up and fought City Hall. No one in this field can say they did that."</p><p>Quinlan said he formed a political advocacy group more than a year ago that raised $1 million to hold neighborhood symposiums and study the issues confronting Chicago. He has roughly $600,000 of that money left and added another $250,000 in campaign contributions just this week.</p><p>"We're the only person willing to run that... doesn't care about doing anything else, and we don't owe anything to anybody else. We're not part of the system. I'm not an elected person. I don't deal with special interests. I'm a lawyer and a very, very good lawyer," Quinlan said.</p><p>"What Chicago needs, given its financial crisis, is someone who will make tough choices on behalf of the residents — not on trying to get re-elected."</p><p>Quinlan joins a crowded field of candidates that already includes eleven other challengers vying to turn Johnson into Chicago’s second straight, one-term mayor. But Quinlan hopes to stand out in the crowd by being free from political baggage.</p><p>"That's what differentiates. You have people who want to make a name for themselves, or they're part of the political group that have been running for multiple offices and they're looking to get re-elected," Quinlan said. "What we're offering is someone who's willing to think about the residents — not the million-dollar donors."</p><p>After the arrest of Blagojevich, Quinlan quit his job as general counsel, saying the embarrassment shattered his "desire to work in public service" ever again. </p><p>"At that time, I was watching a situation that had such great hope. And I felt like that hope wasn't achieved," Quinlan said of his work for Blagojevich, whose 14-year sentence was commuted by President Donald Trump after eight years in prison.</p><p>"Now I'm a little older, a little more thoughtful. We have an obligation to use our talents to help others. We can't sit idle anymore and talk about how the city can do better and watch the same people doing the same thing... for the same special interest over and over and over. The system is broken. We need to fix it."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/13/who-is-running-for-chicago-mayor-2027-election" >Who’s vying to be mayor of Chicago? Here’s a look at the roster of candidates so far</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: White Sox recall Noah Schultz, designated Jose Urquidy for assignment
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND – The White Sox have long promised that rookie left-hander Noah Schultz would play a role on the major league team down the stretch, even as the remaining days left on the regular season calendar continued to thin.</p><p>Putting him on the roster is a pretty crucial first step, and the Sox recalled the 23-year-old Schultz on Tuesday, designating Jose Urquidy for assignment as the corresponding move. Neither Urquidy nor Schultz have pitched in the past week, so the latter should be fresh and ready to contribute, albeit in a role that has yet to be defined.</p><p>Schultz’s last appearance in the majors was on Aug. 7 against the Cleveland Guardians, in an outing where manager Will Venable accidentally had to pull him with one out in the first, because he didn’t realize he was making the second mound visit of the inning. The two runs Schultz allowed that night spiked his major league ERA to 6.06 on the year, but he’s run a 1.66 ERA in his five Triple-A outings since. The rub is that none of those appearances were longer than five innings, nor 70 pitches, and Schultz–whose stuff was diminished near the end of last stint in Chicago–struck out just 10 batters in those 21 ⅔ innings of work.</p><p>At this point of the year, the Sox might not be asking Schultz, or anyone for outings much longer than two turns through the opposing lineup.</p><p>“It’d be great if they go out there and are able to navigate the fifth or sixth inning or more, that’d be fantastic,” general manager Chris Getz said of his starting pitchers on Monday. “But if they don’t, we’ve got other pathways to get to the finish line.”</p><p>With seven pitchers on the Sox active roster who have worked predominantly in starter or bulk innings roles this year, and the coaching staff preaching flexibility across the pitching staff, Schultz could be used in non-traditional fashion. But now he’s once more part of the mix, as will fellow rookie David Sandlin down the stretch. After working to use his sweeper to change eye levels against left-handed hitters, and mixing in his cutter to get opponents off his fastball, Sandlin retired the first 16 batters he faced on Sunday.</p><p>The Sox are sketching out their rotation on a series-to-series basis, but Venable was willing to commit to Sandlin getting another significant opportunity over the season’s final 12 games.</p><p>“He was as effective as anyone we’ve seen here in a little while,” Venable said. “I think it’s very much in our best interest to keep him around.”</p>

entries.title: City Council leaders broker compromise on parking meters, focus of the deal Chicagoans love to hate
entries.summary: <p>City Council leaders have brokered a proposed deal that could pave the way for approval of a New York investment firm to acquire Chicago's parking meters for $2.5 billion, in exchange for a host of lucrative benefits for the city and motorists.</p><p>Former Mayor Rahm Emanuel once tweaked Chicago’s widely despised parking meter deal with a free Sunday parking provision that, as he put it, made “lemonade out of lemons.”</p><p>The agreement quietly brokered with New York-based <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/05/18/chicagos-parking-meters-could-be-sold-again-under-deal-requiring-city-council-approval" >Stonepeak Partners</a> by some of the same alderpersons who led the budget rebellion against Mayor Brandon Johnson’s corporate head tax makes Emanuel’s compromise pale by comparison.</p><p>It includes tangible benefits that could chip away at the city’s $882 million budget gap and create a new revenue stream that would benefit the city for years to come.</p><p>Included in the deal is a proposed profit-sharing arrangement equal to 5% of net income received by Stonepeak and its operating entity, Chicago Parking Meters LLC. That is expected to produce $376.2 million for the city over the course of the agreement, which expires in 2083. That larger payment will also be earmarked for underfunded city pensions.</p><p>The city's Law Department provided technical assistance to the five-member City Council negotiating team. Aside from that, however, the mayor was a bystander.</p><p>“I wouldn’t say it evens the playing field. An even playing field would be — we would still have the asset. But that is not the reality of the situation. So we are making lemonade out of lemons,” Finance Committee Chair and 3rd Ward Ald. Pat Dowell told the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>“It’s a much better deal for the city and for taxpayers. Several elements of the proposal did not exist in the previous proposal. Things like profit-sharing and transfer fees. Collecting revenue when they overcharge us. We were able to increase the amount of time that we get to look at a transfer in the future if it happens. Getting them to focus on electric vehicle charging, then being able to split that revenue with the company,” Dowell said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Chicagoans have grown to hate the deal made under Mayor Richard M. Daley that sold off the city’s on-street parking spots. Here, a driver pays for parking on ParkChicago’s parking machine on North Clark Street in Andersonville on Tuesday. The sale of that lease gave the city the opening it needed to extract a better deal for taxpayers.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Johnson submitted a<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/brandon-johnson/2026/07/10/johnson-finally-explains-his-decision-to-bid-3-2b-for-parking-meters-before-walking-away" > $3.2 billion bid</a> to take back Chicago parking meters, only to abandon it after determining the risk of undoing the parking meter deal Chicagoans love to hate was not worth the reward, either financially or politically.</p><p>The mayor then threw the hot potato to the City Council without providing any guidance about Stonepeak’s bid.</p><p>“We didn’t go around him. Remember, he said the responsibility for approving or disapproving the sale was within the City Council’s hands,” Dowell said Tuesday. “So we took the bull by the horns and did the work.”</p><p>If and when the deal closes, Stonepeak has agreed to pay the city a $75 million transfer fee earmarked for city employee pension funds hovering dangerously close to insolvency. If Stonepeak ever sells the meters to another buyer, Chicago would receive an additional transfer fee of 2% of the sale price — also earmarked for pensions.</p><p> </p><p>The proposal also includes changes to the portion of the lopsided parking meter deal that requires the city to compensate Chicago Parking Meters LLC for every parking space taken out of service either for a special event or construction project. Chicago Parking Meters LLC is the private investment consortium formed by Morgan Stanley, Allianz and Sovereign Wealth Fund of Abu Dhabi.</p><p>A “temporary event closure” plan would allow for seven city events each year, and the “hourly threshold for closure payments” from the city would increase from six hours to ten hours.</p><p>And if true-up payments are due, they would be made to Chicago Parking Meters from “available settlement credits” or from “convenience fee or reserve meter revenues” that don’t drain city coffers.</p><p>The City Council’s Latino Caucus united in opposition to Stonepeak because of the company’s 2025 acquisition of Omni Air International, which has provided long haul deportation flights for the Department of Homeland Security during President Donald Trump's deportation campaign.</p><p>To appease Hispanic alderpersons, Stonepeak committed to selling Omni Air International and said it would confirm the sale with a “certified document following federal approvals.”</p><p>Entire nonmetered city blocks could be designated as sites for electric vehicle charging stations, with charging revenues shared with the city.</p><p>The parking meters deal occurred under Mayor Richard M. Daley, who leased the city's 36,000 parking meters for 75 years to a private consortium for $1.15 billion. He used those proceeds to avoid raising property taxes at a time when city employee pension funds were sinking deeper in the hole. The deal became a political nightmare for later mayors, and for the City Council members who gave it lightning-fast approval.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-9b0000" name="image-9b0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5937496/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc4%2F2b%2F99a972394e7f85dc38f8930b1572%2Fparkingmetercompromise-260916-10.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/038140a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc4%2F2b%2F99a972394e7f85dc38f8930b1572%2Fparkingmetercompromise-260916-10.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/adf1c48/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc4%2F2b%2F99a972394e7f85dc38f8930b1572%2Fparkingmetercompromise-260916-10.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Traffic speeds by a ParkChicago payment machine on North Clark Street in Andersonville on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. A new compromise deal announced Tuesday would give the city a bigger cut of revenue from on-street parking. The city leased the spots to a private operator on a 75-year lease under Mayor Richard M. Daley, who left office in 2011. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Former Finance Chair Scott Waguespack (32nd) cast one of only five “no” votes against the original, lopsided parking meter deal. He has long said there was virtually no chance to change what he called the “ironclad” deal that already has allowed private investors from as far away as Abu Dhabi to nearly double their $1.15 billion outlay with 57 years to go on the original deal.</p><p>But Waguespack told the Sun-Times he was thrilled to be proven wrong after being tapped as one of five alderpersons to lead the talks.</p><p>"For the first time in the [history] of this contract, we've been able to break it open and negotiate some pieces that I would have never thought we were able to before," Waguespack said. "We've come up with a deal that not only is great for taxpayers; it will set the tone for future deals."</p><p>Waguespack stressed the profit-sharing windfall must be earmarked for pension costs, and said that guarantee would be built into the ordinance.</p><p>"The one thing we don't want is for aldermen to think this is something where everybody can just reach in and take what they want," Waguespack said. "This goes directly to reducing the burden on taxpayers by putting it into the pensions."</p><p>Johnson played no role in the negotiations. He was briefed Friday on the compromise.</p><p>During a news conference Tuesday, the mayor welcomed the apparent financial benefits, but stopped short of recommending City Council approval.</p><p>"It was my responsibility to make sure that I created at least a framework of what was possible," Johnson said. "There were some people who didn't believe that we could have a package that provided a much better deal for taxpayers. This was a horrible deal. We know that. Previous administrations have attempted to find a pathway and were not able to." </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/e8bye7-I1CY?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Do you know where your change goes when you park your car at a meter?"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Pritzker extends disaster proclamation to aid recovery from August storms
entries.summary: <p>Gov. JB Pritzker has extended an emergency proclamation for Illinois during severe weather over the summer while also requesting federal funds to help with recovery.</p><p>Pritzker signed a follow-up<u> disaster proclamation</u> extending for another 30 days the one <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/18/pritzker-signs-disaster-proclamation-to-aid-recovery-after-months-of-relentless-and-unprecedented-storms" target="_blank" ><u>signed on Aug. 18</u></a> that frees up more state funds and resources for those impacted by weeks of flooding, tornadoes, and other severe weather. It also expedites the contract and procurement process for local governments to help speed recovery efforts.</p><p>The governor remained confident the request for federal money would be granted despite a failed attempt by the Trump administration to block <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/09/24/illinois-wins-suit-on-disaster-relief-funding-held-by-dhs-over-sanctuary-laws" target="_blank" ><u>$2 billion in disaster relief funding</u></a> over the state’s sanctuary policies last year.</p><p>“Given the scale and severity of destruction in communities across our state, I fully expect our request for FEMA aid to be granted,” Pritzker said in a statement. “Illinoisans are incredibly resilient, but our state should not have to face this recovery alone.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/18/pritzker-signs-disaster-proclamation-to-aid-recovery-after-months-of-relentless-and-unprecedented-storms" >Pritzker signs disaster proclamation to aid recovery after months of ‘relentless and unprecedented’ storms</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/09/24/illinois-wins-suit-on-disaster-relief-funding-held-by-dhs-over-sanctuary-laws" >Illinois, 20 other states win suit on disaster relief funding held up by Trump over ‘sanctuary’ laws</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/08/27/200-tornadoes-illinois-2026" >Why have more than 200 tornadoes hit Illinois this year?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Due to the earlier proclamation, state agencies have been assisting with damage assessments, debris cleanup, power restoration, and mutual aid in several counties, according to the statement.</p><p>But if the federal appeal for money is granted, it would open up temporary housing and home repair grants, low-cost loans for uninsured property damage, and “other programs to help individuals and business owners recover from the effects of this severe weather.”</p><p>That request would apply to residents of the following counties related to that day’s storms: Champaign County, Aug. 13; Cook County, Aug.11; Ford County, Aug. 14-15; Fulton County, Aug. 13-15; McLean County, Aug. 13; Tazewell County, Aug. 13-15; Vermilion County, Aug. 13-15; and Will County, Aug. 11.</p><p>Federal assistance is already available for some who bore the brunt of the storm.</p><p>Smaller and rural communities can qualify for the Community Development Block Grant <a class="Link" href="https://prezlymail.com/c/622eb4c1-4215-4b4e-a7df-0b37a91d0426/0e18f1a2/https%3A%2F%2Fdceo.illinois.gov%2Fcommunitydevelopment%2Fpublicinfrastructuresetaside.html" target="_blank" ><u>Disaster Response</u></a> program, funded by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. It offers up to $250,000 for local governments affected by the disaster, according to Pritzker’s office. Residents have six months from the day of the original declaration last month to apply for assistance.</p><p>It comes months after he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/06/30/pritzker-disaster-proclamation-tornado-flood" target="_blank" ><u>made a similar declaration</u></a> following rounds of severe storms in April and June. More than <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/13/5-tornadoes-confirmed-illinois-total-25-tuesday-storms" target="_blank" ><u>200 tornadoes</u></a> have ravaged the state this year. </p>

entries.title: Thrilling Chicago, Pete Crow-Armstrong, Caleb Williams ‘want to give people something to look forward to’
entries.summary: <p>After <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/13/bears-inactives-vs-panthers-for-week-1-backup-qb-tyson-bagent-inactive-but-designated-as-emergency-3rd-qb" >a wild season-opener</a>, <b>Caleb Williams</b> and the Bears have the Chicago area making Super Bowl plans.</p><p>The city’s hoping <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/15/connor-bedard-blackhawks-captain-best-player-face-of-franchise-leadership" >new Blackhawks captain</a> <b>Connor Bedard</b> will be handed the Stanley Cup one day.</p><p><b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> is on the verge of a 40-40 season, with his Cubs still eyeing a World Series win.</p><p>And that’s this week.</p><p>It might just be <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/04/cubs-bears-bulls-chicago-sports-pete-crow-armstrong-caleb-williams-caleb-wilson-matas-buzelis" >that new era in Chicago sports</a>.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong started Tuesday just three stolen bases away from doing something that’s only been done six times previously in baseball history. He’s the MVP favorite in the regular season’s closing days, with his eyes squarely on what the Cubs can do once the lights get brighter in October.</p><p>You know, the same month when Williams will be slinging it on Sundays and Bedard’s Blackhawks will be in the opening days of their new campaign.</p><p>If you’re a sports fan, this is one of the best times of the year.</p><p>If you’re a Chicago sports fan these days, maybe even more so.</p><p>“We love this part of the year,” Crow-Armstrong said after Monday’s win over the Braves. “Not every city gets to look forward to all four major sports in such a small window like we get to here.</p><p>“We pay a lot of attention. I’m staying in here as long as possible pregame while Sunday football is going on.”</p><p>Crow-Armstrong is coming at Bears season a little differently than most of the city’s football fans.</p><p>He’s friends with Williams, and the quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/03/pete-crow-armstrong-nl-player-of-the-month-august-alex-bregman-stats-kevin-gausman-brewers" >showed up to a Cubs game last month</a> with Bulls stars <b>Matas Buzelis</b> and <b>Caleb Wilson</b>, supporting Crow-Armstrong and watching him homer from behind the Cubs’ dugout.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong has shown up on the sidelines at Soldier Field, too, and the pair’s friendship — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/01/19/blackhawks-jets-caleb-williams-pete-crow-armstrong-connor-bedard-jonathan-toews" >they took in a Blackhawks game</a> earlier this year — only draws more attention to what the city’s two biggest sports stars and their contemporaries are capable of.</p><p>“It still kind of is trippy, but it’s cool that people appreciate us being friends,” Crow-Armstrong said. “We’ve definitely talked about what we want to build here together. But that all stems from a genuine appreciation of each other’s abilities and craft and how we make stuff happen.</p><p>“It’s agreed upon by all of us that we want to give people something to look forward to.”</p><h3><b>Miller out of time</b></h3><p>The Cubs are shutting down righty reliever <b>Shelby Miller</b>, who was working back from elbow surgery and was speculated as someone who could help the bullpen.</p><p>But Miller won’t be making an 11th-hour return to the majors this year, even after impressing the Cubs with his relatively speedy recovery; he was signed to a two-year deal without much expectation that he’d pitch this season.</p><p>Miller, a 13-year major league vet who posted a 2.74 ERA with the Diamondbacks and Brewers last season, had a 7.59 ERA in 13 minor league rehab appearances.</p><p>“At this point, the risk outweighs what reward there would be from keeping him going and pushing him to pitch in this environment,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said Tuesday. “It’s just a risk that we agreed together not to take.</p><p>“We’ve got a healthy player, we’ve got a player ready for spring training going into next season, and we’re excited about that.</p><p>“He’s in a good spot. But he’s in a spot that you’re at after you’ve worked your butt off to get there. It’s time to stop and just give him a break.”</p><h3><b>Rained out</b></h3><p>A Tuesday rainout prevented shortstop <b>Dansby Swanson</b> from beginning his minor league rehab assignment with Triple-A Iowa. The Cubs were hoping Swanson would play in a couple games and return to the big league team Friday.</p>

entries.title: Homeless man gets 60 years for fatally stabbing visiting grad student in the Loop
entries.summary: <p>Tony Robinson, a homeless man who fatally stabbed visiting graduate student Anat Kimchi in 2021 as she walked in the Loop, was sentenced Tuesday to the maximum allowed — 60 years in prison.</p><p>Cook County Circuit Judge John F. Lyke Jr. said the murder was a “heinous, senseless and brutal crime” that took the life of a gifted criminal justice researcher “whose vision was to improve the very system that we are a part of.”</p><p>The sentencing capped a bizarre hearing Tuesday morning that featured emotional testimony from family members, friends and academic colleagues, as well as meandering rants from Robinson, who fired his public defenders and opted to represent himself.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a </div><p>The hearing also featured gripping testimony from a downstate woman who identified Robinson as the man who bashed her over the head with a sock full of rocks, breaking her nose and requiring stitches and staples for her head injuries, just six days before the attack on Kimchi.</p><p>A jury in May <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/14/anat-kimchi-verdict-loop-stabbing-death-tony-robinson-trial-guilty-verdict" target="_blank" ><u>convicted Robinson</u></a>, 46, of murdering Kimchi, 31, a University of Maryland doctoral student who was visiting a friend in Chicago. The attack happened June 19, 2021, on a sunny Saturday afternoon, as Kimchi looked for a place to sit and read a book.</p><p>As Kimchi walked in the 400 block of South Wacker Drive, just south of the Willis Tower, Robinson sneaked up behind her and stabbed her three times in her neck and back.</p><p>More than five years after her daughter’s murder, Chava Kimchi-Sarfaty finally got to make her victim impact statement. She talked about how Anat called her nearly every morning as she walked her dog.</p><p>“I miss this morning call so much. You can’t imagine how much,” she said. “It used to be one of the things I most looked forward to when I woke up. I can’t say I even really wake up these days because my nights are spent thinking about Anat’s last minutes and 'what if’ questions that would never be answered.”</p><p>She added: “Every wedding I attend, I think of how I will never be able to walk Anat down the aisle. Every new child that is born, I think I will never be able to hold her child in my arms.”</p><p>Kimchi’s father, Avraham Kimchi, read a poem about his daughter.</p><p>“Anat always teased me that she will help me find things to do as I grow old. And she kept her promise — all our family, together with her colleagues, are committed to continue Anat’s legacy and find ways to improve our justice system,” he said.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Anat Kimchi’s brothers Itamar and Ofer also spoke. Ofer, his voice breaking, began by explaining his sorrow that she’ll never meet her nephew, his son.</p><p>“When Anat was murdered, I lost the person I was. I used to believe in God. How can I express that loss?” he asked.</p><p>“I rarely feel safe anymore. When I’m in public, even when I’m at home, I think about how I, or the people I love, can die at any moment. I know how important it is for my son to grow up feeling safe and secure, but I don’t know how to help him feel safe when I know that behind those trees, there might be a man with a knife and the intent to murder.”</p><p>Robinson, wearing a tan jail uniform, leaned back in a chair at the defense table, a sheriff’s officer close by. Occasionally, he sneezed or coughed.</p><p>Much of the testimony focused on the irony that Kimchi’s research aimed to uncover disparities in the criminal justice system and make it better.</p><p>By all accounts a brilliant yet humble student, she had earned two undergraduate degrees and a master’s from the University of Maryland. Two weeks after her death, she was posthumously awarded her doctorate.</p><p>Much of Kimchi’s data-driven research focused on how offenders’ race and ethnicity were predictive of their probation conditions. She found Black probationers were more likely to get tougher conditions, leading to a higher likelihood of violations.</p><p>Lyke said Kimchi's supporters gave “some of the more powerful victim impact statements I’ve ever heard, in over 30 years in the criminal justice system.”</p><p>The attack was one of several shocking cases examined in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/chicago-downtown-attacks-mental-health-system" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Sun-Times investigation</u></a> last year into violent attacks Downtown.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-820001" name="module-820001"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h4><b>FAILURE TO TREAT, FAILURE TO PROTECT</b></h4><i>This investigation by the Sun-Times examines how the failures of the mental health system in Chicago have had deadly consequences and looks at possible solutions.</i><br><h5><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/chicago-downtown-attacks-mental-health-system" >Read more stories in the series > </a></h5></div> </div><p>Robinson lived in a tent on Lower Wacker Drive. According to police and court records, he had a history of arrests and bizarre behavior, including telling detectives that he believed people were tracking him with their cellphones.</p><p>At Tuesday’s hearing, Nicole Ferguson, 56, of Mattoon, testified that on the morning of June 13, 2021, she was leaving a Downtown hotel to get coffee when Robinson came out of an alley and asked, “Are you following me, b----?”</p><p>She said she replied “no” and looked back at her phone, then glimpsed a long, dark-colored object out of the corner of her eye.</p><p>“It hit me in the head very hard. Before I could even turn around, I was hit again,” she testified.</p><p>Her money and phone fell to the ground, and she was struck a third time. She said Robinson grabbed her belongings, and she was taken to a hospital.</p><p>Police later recovered a black sock filled with rocks in Robinson’s tent.</p><p>Mental illness never came up at the hearing. Robinson simply claimed he didn’t do it.</p><p>At the trial, prosecutors did not have video of Kimchi's murder, but they <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/05/13/anat-kimchi-tony-robinson-murder-trial-chicago" target="_blank" >showed numerous clips</a> of Robinson sneaking up on Kimchi, running from the scene with a knife, throwing an object into the river and changing his shirt. An eyewitness — another homeless man who called 911 — testified that he later confronted Robinson at his tent and that Robinson <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/05/11/cook-county-murder-trial-tony-robinson-anat-kimchi-graduate-student-university-maryland" target="_blank" >menaced him with a entries.title: Tofu replaces meat in vegetarian satay skewers packed with plenty of flavor and texture
entries.summary: <p>Satay is one of Southeast Asia's most recognizable grilled street foods, sold everywhere from roadside carts and night markets to family-run restaurants. While many people associate satay with Indonesia, versions of the dish are also enjoyed across Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and other parts of the region, each with its own marinades, seasonings and accompaniments. What unites them is the method, in which small pieces of marinated protein are threaded onto skewers and grilled over hot charcoal, where the smoke and intense heat create deeply flavorful, succulent, crispy bites.</p><p>Traditional satay is often made with meat, such as chicken, beef or lamb. In this vegetarian version, extra-firm tofu replaces the meat. Tofu's mild flavor and porous texture, along with the initial step of pressing it first, allow it to readily absorb the marinade. The grill adds smoky notes and ensures charred edges, resulting in a delicious skewer with plenty of flavor and texture.</p><p>Don't overlook the peanut dipping sauce. It's a recipe worth keeping on repeat. Creamy, sweet and spicy, it complements the skewers and is equally delicious when drizzled over cold noodle salads, spooned onto grain bowls or served alongside fresh spring rolls and crisp vegetables. Refrigerate any leftovers for up to one week.</p><h3>Tofu Satay Skewers With Peanut Sauce</h3><p><b>Prep time:</b> 30 minutes<br><b>Total time:</b> 30 minutes, plus pressing and marinating time<br><b>Yield:</b> Serves 3 to 4</p><p><b>Ingredients</b></p><p>M<b>arinade</b><br>3 tablespoons soy sauce or tamari<br>2 tablespoons toasted sesame oil<br>1 garlic clove, grated<br>1 tablespoon maple syrup<br>1 tablespoon lime juice<br>1 teaspoon finely grated peeled fresh ginger<br>1 teaspoon Asian hot sauce, such as Sriracha</p><p><b>Sauce</b><br>1/3 cup creamy peanut butter<br>2 tablespoons water<br>1 1/2 tablespoons soy sauce or tamari<br>1 tablespoon maple syrup<br>1 tablespoon fresh lime juice<br>1 teaspoon finely grated peeled fresh ginger<br>1 garlic clove, grated<br>1 teaspoon Asian hot sauce, such as Sriracha</p><p><b>Tofu</b><br>1 (14-ounce) package extra-firm tofu<br>Vegetable oil for the griddle<br>Chopped peanuts, for garnish<br>Chopped fresh cilantro leaves, for garnish<br>Lime wedges, for serving</p><p>Special equipment: 6 to 8 (8-inch) bamboo skewers, pre-soaked in warm water for 30 minutes</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Combine the marinade ingredients in a bowl and whisk to blend.</p><p>In a separate bowl, combine the sauce ingredients and whisk until smooth.</p><p>Cut the tofu block into 3/4- to 1-inch-thick slices. Place the tofu slices on a cutting board lined with paper towels or a kitchen towel. Place several layers of paper towels on top, or fold the towel over the tofu. Place a cutting board on top of the tofu and place a heavy object, such as a kitchen pan, on top. Let stand for 20 to 30 minutes to drain.</p><p>Once pressed, cut the tofu slices into 3/4- to 1-inch cubes. Arrange the tofu in one layer in a baking dish. Pour the marinade over and turn the tofu to coat. Refrigerate for 30 minutes to 1 hour, turning once or twice.</p><p>When ready to grill, remove the tofu from the marinade and thread on the bamboo skewers.</p><p>Heat a griddle on the grill over direct medium heat for 10 minutes.</p><p>Lightly oil the griddle. Cook the skewers on the griddle until golden brown on all sides, about 6 to 8 minutes, turning with tongs to evenly cook.</p><p>Transfer the skewers to a platter. Garnish with the peanuts and/or cilantro. Serve with the peanut sauce and lime wedges.</p><p><i>Lynda Balslev is an award-winning writer, cookbook author and recipe developer, and authors the blog TasteFood.</i></p>

entries.title: Who’s vying to be mayor of Chicago? Here’s a look at the roster of candidates so far

</div><p></p><h3>Mayor Brandon Johnson</h3><p>With a 30% public approval rating and less than $650,000 in his campaign fund, Johnson, 50, is in real danger of becoming Chicago’s second straight one-term mayor. But Johnson has a solid base in the African-American community, and hence a strong chance of making the runoff. He has also delivered on key progressive promises like paid leave, while proposing protections for renters struggling with affordability. But he’s likely to have a much tougher time reaching the 50%-plus-one vote tally he needs to win a second term. The coalition of progressive unions that bankrolled and staffed Johnson’s winning campaign has fractured. The Chicago Teachers Union, where Johnson served as a paid organizer, remains firmly in the mayor’s camp. But the Service Employees International Union and its affiliates are expected to either remain neutral or endorse Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ec0000" name="image-ec0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7e3321c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7828x4393+0+414/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F55%2F674af5a1400b929a9ff1b43da80c%2Ffranshow-260803-005.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1084db8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7828x4393+0+414/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F55%2F674af5a1400b929a9ff1b43da80c%2Ffranshow-260803-005.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2c2616b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7828x4393+0+414/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F55%2F674af5a1400b929a9ff1b43da80c%2Ffranshow-260803-005.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias announces his run for mayor at an event in Bronzeville on the South Side on Aug. 2, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2c2616b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7828x4393+0+414/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F55%2F674af5a1400b929a9ff1b43da80c%2Ffranshow-260803-005.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/544c587/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7828x4393+0+414/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F55%2F674af5a1400b929a9ff1b43da80c%2Ffranshow-260803-005.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2c2616b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7828x4393+0+414/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F55%2F674af5a1400b929a9ff1b43da80c%2Ffranshow-260803-005.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias announces his run for mayor at an event in Bronzeville on Aug. 2.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Alexi Giannoulias</h3><p>Business leaders and building trade unions have rallied behind the 50-year-old Illinois Secretary of State, helping Giannoulias amass a $22 million campaign war chest that makes him the presumed frontrunner. That also puts a political target on Giannoulias’ back. The controversy surrounding the failure of Broadway Bank, a now-shuttered institution once owned by the Giannoulias family, is almost certain to be resurrected. Giannoulias, a basketball-playing buddy of former President Barack Obama who played professional basketball in Greece, will also need to prove he has the political gravitas to handle the job of mayor.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-800000" name="image-800000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/680854a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5762x3234+0+304/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2Fdb%2Fb997f0264515bfb4e12341f6bd5a%2Fstatefairdem-260620-18.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/49cca6f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5762x3234+0+304/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2Fdb%2Fb997f0264515bfb4e12341f6bd5a%2Fstatefairdem-260620-18.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2e4c7ae/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5762x3234+0+304/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2Fdb%2Fb997f0264515bfb4e12341f6bd5a%2Fstatefairdem-260620-18.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Illinois State Comptroller Susana Mendoza, who is running for mayor of Chicago, speaks during the Illinois Democratic County Chairs’ brunch at the Bank of Springfield Center in Springfield, Ill., Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2e4c7ae/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5762x3234+0+304/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2Fdb%2Fb997f0264515bfb4e12341f6bd5a%2Fstatefairdem-260620-18.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/24e3f1a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5762x3234+0+304/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2Fdb%2Fb997f0264515bfb4e12341f6bd5a%2Fstatefairdem-260620-18.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2e4c7ae/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5762x3234+0+304/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdd%2Fdb%2Fb997f0264515bfb4e12341f6bd5a%2Fstatefairdem-260620-18.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Illinois State Comptroller Susana Mendoza, a candidate for mayor of Chicago, speaks at the Illinois Democratic County Chairs’ brunch, held Aug. 19 at the Bank of Springfield Center in Springfield.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Susana Mendoza</h3><p>Unlike Giannoulias, who is simultaneously running for re-election as Secretary of State, the 54-year-old Mendoza is all-in. She’s giving up her job as state comptroller to make her second run for mayor. Mendoza finished fifth in a 2019 mayoral race won by Lori Lightfoot and dominated by the corruption scandal that culminated in the conviction of Ald. Edward Burke (14th). Wilson's endorsement of Lightfoot sent a signal to his older, church-based constituency that, as he put it, "contracts and jobs and schools" were more important than concerns they may have about Lightfoot being gay. Wilson called his endorsement of Lightfoot "a hell of a mistake." Four years later, he made another political mistake by endorsing Paul Vallas, who lost to Brandon Johnson. An ardent supporter of Trump, Carter-Walters has been an outspoken critic of Chicago’s sanctuary city ordinance. She has also advocated for calling in the National Guard to combat violent crime in Chicago.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7c0000" name="image-7c0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/46bb5f3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6370x3575+0+336/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2F8d%2Ffaa403e243f6b7579c391b54c009%2Fpedrocourt-122524-2.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d349c6b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6370x3575+0+336/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2F8d%2Ffaa403e243f6b7579c391b54c009%2Fpedrocourt-122524-2.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ab28631/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6370x3575+0+336/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe9%2F8d%2Ffaa403e243f6b7579c391b54c009%2Fpedrocourt-122524-2.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="William J. Behind him is then Chicago Public Schools CEO Pedro Martinez. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>William J. Quinlan</h3><p>The son and namesake of former Mayor Richard J. Daley’s corporation counsel, Quinlan, 56, had a front-row seat to the inner workings of City Hall politics. But the Northwest Side lawyer is running for mayor as a reformer who “owes no one” and “understands the system, but is not part of the system.” It could be a tough sell with Chicago voters. Quinlan spent three years as general counsel for Illinois under then-Gov. Rod Blagojevich. When Blagojevich was arrested on corruption charges, Quinlan left public service saying the embarrassment had shattered his “desire to work in public service” ever again. He went on to serve as an election attorney for leading Democrats in Illinois and across the nation. Asked why he changed his mind about public service, Quinlan pointed to the devastating family tragedy he suffered during childhood. His mother and younger brother were killed in a fire at the Quinlan family’s Sauganash home. Another brother died after struggling with mental illness and “navigating a fragmented system of care… I lost many, many family members in tragic circumstances. And I realized that life is to be cherished. It comes with an obligation to give back.”<br></p>

entries.title: Five needles the next WNBA commissioner will have to thread
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> guard Natasha Cloud <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/09/10/skys-natasha-cloud-knows-what-she-wants-in-the-next-wnba-commissioner" target="_blank" >told the Sun-Times</a> last week she wants the next WNBA commissioner to be a former player, preferably from a minority group, who better will protect players from the hazards of mainstream attention.</p><p>Teammate Elizabeth Williams, the secretary of the players’ union, offered broader criteria: ‘‘some knowledge of the WNBA at some level’’ and ‘‘some level of business knowledge … as well.’’</p><p>Sounds reasonable enough.</p><p>The new commissioner will inherit a much stronger league than Cathy Engelbert did in 2019, but it still has a long way to go. And in part because it remains under the NBA’s control, improvements rarely come easily.</p><p>Here are five needles the commissioner will have to thread to help the league realize its potential.</p><h3>1. Expansion</h3><p>The WNBA will grow to 18 teams by the end of the decade, up from 12 at the beginning of it. How many more can be added without diluting the quality of play? The commissioner should have some intuition about the answer to that question and a rigorous approach to answering it fully.</p><p>The commissioner should recognize recent expansion has succeeded partly because excellent international players have helped to fill out the new rosters. The priority should be continuing to attract those players by raising salaries and staying flexible around the FIBA schedule.</p><h3>2. Scheduling</h3><p>Adding teams will mean more games, which will be great for fans and TV partners. But how do you add games while working within the NBA’s vision for the ‘‘W’’ as a complementary summer league? Players are wary about cramming too many games into too short a period.</p><p>The commissioner either will have to create more time out of thin air or become an agitator and persuade the NBA to let the league move to a winter schedule. NBA teams might resist sharing their arenas or TV windows, but the change would create a more sustainable calendar.</p><h3>3. Officiating</h3><p>The good news is that the most prominent critic of the officiating last year, Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve, thinks there has been progress this season. But the system is still flawed. WNBA officials train in the NBA’s developmental league before transitioning to the women’s game — an arrangement that makes little sense — and are paid far less. The commissioner will have to persuade stakeholders to pony up and fix the system.</p><p>The commissioner also will have to build more of a consensus around what kind of game everyone wants to see. Reeve and her superstar, Napheesa Collier, want a greater emphasis on freedom of movement — in other words, officiating that favors the offensive player. Cloud, on the other hand, told the Sun-Times she prefers a game that allows defenders to be more physical. And she’s not the only one.</p><h3>4. Resource disparity</h3><p>The gap between how the best and worst franchises operate is still pretty wacky. The Valkyries sell out all 18,000 seats for every game, while the Mystics play in what feels like a high school gym. The Mercury practice in a dedicated $100 million facility, while the Sky rotate between college gyms.</p><p>The new collective-bargaining agreement establishes minimum standards for resources, which should eliminate the truly embarrassing situations. But a commissioner also should have a vision for creating more uniformity across the board.</p><h3>5. Public acceptance</h3><p>The chaos surrounding the league during its ascent has shown how much difficulty the public is having accepting professional women’s basketball as big business. The commissioner will have to coach everyone through it.</p><p>Sometimes, that should be fun: storytelling and promoting a beautiful game.</p><p>Other times, it won’t be so fun: condemning threats and abuse and protecting players. Many think Engelbert fell short there, but NBC’s Jackie Powell recently reported that her reactive approach was partly in deference to league lawyers weighing the NBA’s interests.</p><p>Any commissioner must be capable of the diplomacy and shape-shifting required to keep owners and players happy. The WNBA commissioner, however, also might need the guts to defy superiors.</p><p>That is the ultimate needle the next commissioner will have to thread: leading the league through this phase of growth, even when its interests conflict with the NBA’s.</p>

entries.title: Man critically injured in Avalon Park shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man was critically injured in a shooting in Avalon Park Tuesday afternoon, according to the Chicago Police Department.</p><p>The victim, 46, was walking to his vehicle in the 8400 block of South Euclid Avenue at 3:45 p.m. when another man opened fire, then fled, police said. </p><p>The man, shot six times, was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center in critical condition.</p><p>No one is in custody, police said. </p>

entries.title: Wait! You mean we don't gotta pay taxes?
entries.summary: <p>Unlike you, I've earned millions of dollars through writing. True, the bulk of that was in modest, regular increments over a 45-year period, mostly salary from this newspaper, where writing is only one of several duties — there is navigating the web of colleagues and superiors, the strategic cordiality, the gossip, the bowing, the scraping, the "yes sir, that is a <i>brilliant</i> idea" side as well.</p><p>Occasionally — very occasionally, of late — freelance checks show up: article payments, book royalties or advances, and I will announce the sum in my best imitation of a stentorian Bill Kurtis proclamation: "Bumpty-bump <i>thousand</i> dollars!" And my wife, God bless her, dutiful sworn officer of the court that she is, will observe, as if on cue: "Of course, you have to pay taxes on that." </p><p>Silly me, I take her at her word. When April 15 comes around, we do indeed pay whatever portion — and it can be between a quarter and a third — that our accountant says is due the federal government. </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6c0000" name="module-6c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>So it was with gratitude that I recently read <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/11/five-things-to-know-about-rachel-cohen-brandon-johnson-communications-director" target="_blank" >in the Sun-Times</a> how Mayor Brandon Johnson's new communications director, Rachel Cohen, deliberately withheld federal income taxes on her freelance work as a protest against ICE. Can we all do that? Because I too have freelance, and I too have serious disagreements with a considerable part of the federal government — the entire executive branch leaps to mind.</p><p>If we can simply withhold our taxes, then not only will I have registered a protest, but saved myself some significant scratch as well, manna I will need on the long slog through retirement, set to begin ... well ... maybe sooner than I care to if I keep turning in stuff like this.</p><p>Don't get me wrong. I'm all for social action. Protests such as last year's at Broadview were not just heroic, but essential. Like colonial minutemen pouring out of their farms and shops to face the British, patriotic Americans poured into the streets to show that we do not want federal thugs grabbing our neighbors out of their cars for the crime of having immigrated to this country, plunging them into some nightmare gulag system, the true horror of which is not yet fully known. We haven't yet saved the United States from despotism, but if it is indeed saved, they deserve ample credit.</p><p>But I'm also a chronic law abider. I can't rip the tag off a new mattress. My fingers tingle seeing how glibly some break the law and get away with it.</p><p>Yes, there is a tradition of tax evasion related to the mayor's office. Mayor Harold Washington, you might recall, did not file his federal taxes for four years in the 1960s — not even as a protest, but due to being disorganized, he later said. The IRS went after him, and though it was determined that he had actually paid the baseline amounts, and only owed $508, that was enough for him to plead no contest and be sentenced to 40 days in the Cook County Jail in 1972, serving 36. </p><p>He "forgot," Washington told the Sun-Times editorial board during his 1983 run, adding "maybe a psychiatrist could explain it." He still won.</p><p>"I'm not proud of this," Washington added, as opposed to Cohen, who seems very proud.</p><p>Will his aide's admitted criminality come to dog Johnson as he battles against long odds — underfinanced and under-popular — for a second term? His chief rival, Alexi Giannoulias, has his own finance-related baggage: His family's Broadway Bank collapsed in a klaxon of allegations, though no criminal charges were filed.</p><p>The mayor does have a reputation for ignoring certain illegalities — teens rampaging through the Loop get an avuncular chuckle when Downtown businesses might prefer the youths hauled off to the clink. And if I ever talk to Rachel Cohen — I actually had lunch with her predecessor, Erin Connelly, which, though pleasant, did not lead to anything in the newspaper — I'll ask what makes her think the money she withheld from the government would have been used to buy shock gloves for ICE? Maybe it was the cash needed to buy milk for preschoolers (Oh wait, we stopped doing that, right?). OK then, to the shrinking part of the federal government that isn't self-dealing and corrupt.</p><p>We'll never speak. The whole reason for hiring an online influencer as communications director is because you want to bypass traditional journalism, avoid anyone who might do that thinky, judgy thing, and go straight to ballyhooing the public directly. Why have your actions parsed by the keen, knowledgeable eye of a Fran Spielman when you can hand Rachel Cohen a pair of pompons and have her leading cheers on social media? Maybe that'll work for him. We'll see.</p>
entries.author: Neil Steinberg
